title: Shango, the King Who Became a Storm
subtitle: A legend and an ethnographer hear the same royal cry

sango.excerpt: worshipped as the god of thunder and lightning. So, among all the Yorubas, when people see the flash of lightning followed by the sullen roar of thunder, they remember Sango’s rage after the destruction of his palace, and exclaim: “Long live the King!”
sango.note: Verbatim English text from M. I. Ogumefu's 1929 collection, which his preface describes as belonging to the Yoruba country of Southern Nigeria. It is a Yoruba-authored retelling for readers, not an ethnographic record of practice.

chant.work: The Yoruba-Speaking Peoples of the Slave Coast of West Africa
chant.author: A. B. Ellis
chant.translator: not applicable; authored in English by A. B. Ellis
chant.locator: Chapter II · CHIEF GODS; Chapter II · CHIEF GODS, normalized characters 21545-22176
chant.excerpt: A chant of the Oni-Shango very commonly heard is, "Oh Shango, thou art the master. Thou takest in thy hand thy fiery stones, to punish the guilty and satisfy thine anger. Everything that they strike is destroyed. Their fire eats up the forest, the trees are broken down, and all living creatures are slain;" and the lay-worshippers of Shango flock into the streets during a thunderstorm crying, "Shango, Shango, Great King! Shango is the lord and master. In the storm he hurls his fiery stones against his enemies, and their track gleams in the midst of the darkness." "May Shango's stone strike you," is a very common imprecation.
chant.note: Verbatim English text from Ellis's 1894 survey of the Yoruba-speaking peoples. It is colonial-era ethnography: claims belong to Ellis's report, and his comparative and evolutionary framing is commentary, not community testimony.

orisha.work: The Yoruba-Speaking Peoples of the Slave Coast of West Africa
orisha.author: A. B. Ellis
orisha.translator: not applicable; authored in English by A. B. Ellis
orisha.locator: Chapter II · CHIEF GODS; Chapter II · CHIEF GODS, normalized characters 1610-2131
orisha.excerpt: The term used by the Yoruba tribes to express a superhuman being, or god, is orisha, and as it is used equally to express the images and sacred objects, and also as an adjective with the meaning of sacred or holy, it answers exactly to the Tshi term bohszon, the Gã wong, and the Ewe vodu. The word orisha seems to be compounded of ori (summit, top, head) and sha (to select, choose); though some natives prefer to derive it from ri (to see) and isha (selection, choice), and thus to make it mean "One who sees the cult."
orisha.note: Verbatim English text from Ellis's 1894 survey of the Yoruba-speaking peoples. It is colonial-era ethnography: claims belong to Ellis's report, and his comparative and evolutionary framing is commentary, not community testimony.

narrativeBlocks.title: A king's terrible charm
narrativeBlocks.body: In Ogumefu's legend, King Sango finds a charm that calls down lightning. He tries it on his own palace; the storm kills his family, his followers desert him, and he ends his life in despair.

narrativeBlocks.title: The people remember a king
narrativeBlocks.body: Source quotation (Yoruba Legends; whitespace normalized): “worshipped as the god of thunder and lightning. So, among all the Yorubas, when people see the flash of lightning followed by the sullen roar of thunder, they remember Sango’s rage after the destruction of his palace, and exclaim: “Long live the King!””

narrativeBlocks.title: An ethnographer hears the same cry
narrativeBlocks.body: Writing in 1894, Ellis reports that Shango's worshippers run into the streets during thunderstorms crying "Shango, Shango, Great King!" A legend explains the cry; the survey records it happening.

narrativeBlocks.title: Two kinds of book, one custom
narrativeBlocks.body: Ogumefu was a Yoruba author publishing legends in 1929; Ellis was a British colonial officer describing religion in 1894. Keep the legend's explanation and the ethnographer's report distinct, and remember Yoruba religion is still practised today.

narrativeBlocks.title: What orisha means
narrativeBlocks.body: Ellis reports that the Yoruba word for a superhuman being or god is orisha, a word also used for sacred images and objects and as an adjective meaning holy. Shango is one orisha among many in his survey.

quiz.prompt: In Ogumefu's legend, what happens after lightning destroys Sango's palace?

choices.text: His friends desert him and he ends his life in despair
He marries the river goddess Oya
He hides in a cave and becomes a soothsayer

quiz.explanation: After the palace burns, Sango's followers desert him one by one until, alone, he puts an end to his life; his people then give him an honourable funeral and worship him as god of thunder.
